summary:
Space Travel is an interactive 3D educational map that lets children explore 31 NASA space missions in chronological order, from Mariner 2 (1962) to Europa Clipper (2024). Each mission has a spacecraft "voice" that greets the child, plus details on dates, destinations, goals, agencies and discoveries. We built it with Spline and Three.js, and used Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot for research and content, with NASA's Eyes on the Solar System as a reference.
The challenge asks us to bring young space enthusiasts closer to NASA's spacecraft and the science behind them. Space Travel tells each mission's story in child-friendly language, from the spacecraft's own perspective, covering missions both completed and still active.
It makes space science accessible, sparks curiosity and scientific thinking, and invites the next generation to explore STEM.
details: iSpace Travel is an interactive 3D map of the solar system where children explore 32 NASA missions in chronological order, from Mariner 2 (1962) to Europa Clipper (2024). Users press "Start," hover over a planet, click to zoom in, and use the arrow keys to move between planets. Each mission opens a card with its dates, destination, agency, purpose and achievement, plus a welcome message told by the spacecraft itself. Benefits It turns complex space science into child-friendly content. It encourages curiosity and scientific thinking, connects history, science and technology, and introduces real missions and discoveries. Expected impact We hope to make space exploration more accessible to primary school children and inspire the next generation to explore STEM fields. Tools, languages and software Languages: JavaScript, HTML and CSS 3D and design: Three.js and Spline AI assistants: Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot, for research, organizing information and writing content Reference: NASA's Eyes on the Solar System and public NASA mission information Publishing: Netlify Creativity Instead of a list of facts, each spacecraft speaks in its own voice ("Hello, I'm Mariner 2!"). This makes children feel they are travelling with every mission. Factors our team considered Accuracy: mission names, dates and discoveries come from our verified mission data. Audience: simple, friendly language for children. NASA guidelines: we avoid NASA logos, flags and mission identifiers, and we credit every external resource. Experience: missions follow chronological order so children can see how exploration advanced.
